canonical_statement: The study evaluates whether direct, interpretable document operations can outperform embedding-mediated top-k retrieval for exactness-critical question answering over a long structured financial report.
The study explicitly aims to measure structural properties of the document and the context loss caused by chunking rather than attributing failure to retrieval tuning alone.
The testbed is the Gujarat Finance Accounts 2024-25, Volume I, a 780-page, 3.97 MB audited government financial report converted to Markdown for retrieval experiments.

The authors selected pymupdf4llm as the PDF-to-Markdown converter after comparing four backends because it preserved row labels with their figures and table-column alignment better than the completed alternatives.
Of 19,198 non-empty lines in the converted report, 16,664 were table rows, corresponding to a table-row fraction of 86.8%.

population.label: Non-empty lines in the converted Gujarat Finance Accounts

canonical_statement: The report contained 58,791 numeric tokens but only 15,960 distinct numeric tokens, a numeric repetition ratio of 3.68-fold.

population.label: Numeric tokens in the converted report

canonical_statement: A numeric table row inherited its governing unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it, with a 90th percentile distance of 26 lines and a maximum distance of 143 lines.

population.label: Numeric table rows in the converted report

concept.text: Distance from numeric row to governing unit header

canonical_statement: Chunking damage was evaluated by defining numeric chunks as unitless when they contained no unit declaration and yearless when they contained no fiscal-year column header, across fixed-size and table-aware chunkers over a five-fold chunk-size range.
With fixed-size 800-character chunks, 67.4% of numeric chunks were unitless and 73.8% were yearless.

population.label: Numeric chunks produced by fixed-size 800-character chunking

canonical_statement: At a 2,000-character target, table-aware chunking reduced unitless numeric chunks from 18.0% under fixed-size chunking to 0.3%, while 28.9% of table-aware numeric chunks remained yearless.
Across table-aware chunk sizes from 800 to 4,000 characters, the fraction of yearless numeric chunks remained between 27.2% and 30.1%, spanning only 2.9 percentage points.

population.label: Numeric chunks generated by the table-aware chunker across the chunk-size sweep

canonical_statement: The table-aware chunker scans backward up to 200 lines at each boundary for the nearest governing unit and fiscal-year rows and prepends them subject to a capped seed budget.

READ exposes deterministic document access through file listing, structural outline, normalized line search, and bounded line reads; read calls are capped at 400 lines and the server is jailed to a root directory.

READ normalized search matches each query against spaced and squashed shadow forms of each line while returning original line numbers, allowing cell boundaries, emphasis markers, whitespace, and thousands separators to be ignored during matching.
In 12 realistic matching probes, normalization changed the retrieval outcome for exactly two query types: an ungrouped numeric figure and a subject phrase split across table cells.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: number of probes whose outcome changed

canonical_statement: The converter-damage audit found 483 artifact instances affecting 440 table rows (2.6%), including 381 numeric rows (3.0%) and 11 numeric rows with magnitude errors (0.09%).

population.label: Table rows in the converted report

quantitative_result.effect_measure: table rows affected by conversion damage (%)

canonical_statement: The authors classify questions whose source values are destroyed during PDF conversion as conversion-limited rather than attributing those failures to the retrieval system, because no retriever can recover information absent from the converted corpus.
All evaluated retrieval systems used gemini-2.5-pro as the generator; dense retrieval used BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5, and the hybrid system added cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 reranking.
The benchmark comprised 51 verified questions: 24 lookup, 9 arithmetic, 6 navigation, 5 aggregation, 5 unanswerable, and 2 conversion-limited questions.

Benchmark admission required mechanical checks for source-figure presence near the declared gold line, column mapping using table arithmetic identities, and confirmation that derived answers did not already appear in the corpus.

Primary evaluation used three independent signals: deterministic exact-figure accuracy, a fixed LLM judge, and a mechanical groundedness check requiring every figure in an answer to appear in text actually retrieved or read.
System comparisons were paired by question, tested with exact McNemar tests, supplemented with paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and Holm-corrected across the baseline family.
READ answered 58.8% of the 51-question benchmark, with a Wilson 95% confidence interval of 45.2% to 71.2%.

outcome.measurement_method: Deterministic numeric comparison with normalization and 0.5% relative tolerance

canonical_statement: The matched dense top-k baseline at 2,000-character table-aware chunks and k=8 answered 15.7% of the benchmark, with a Wilson 95% confidence interval of 8.2% to 28.0%.

outcome.measurement_method: Deterministic numeric comparison with normalization and 0.5% relative tolerance

canonical_statement: READ exceeded the matched dense baseline by 43.1 percentage points in accuracy; the paired 95% confidence interval was 27.5 to 56.9 points and Holm-corrected p was 0.00002.

outcome.measurement_method: Deterministic numeric comparison with normalization and 0.5% relative tolerance

canonical_statement: Agentic RAG, using the same agent loop but a vector-search top-k tool, achieved 27.5% accuracy; READ led it by 31.4 percentage points with Holm-corrected p=0.012.

canonical_statement: Groundedness was 58.0% for READ, 67.3% for BM25, and 72.0% for hybrid retrieval, so READ was not the most grounded system by the study's mechanical metric.
Among five unanswerable probes, dense retrieval answered four (80%), hybrid answered three (60%), READ and BM25 each answered two (40%), and naive-grep and agentic RAG answered none.

canonical_statement: On the nine cross-statement arithmetic questions, READ achieved 44.4% accuracy compared with 11.1% for dense retrieval and 33.3% for BM25.

canonical_statement: Dense retrieval never surfaced the gold evidence on 13 of 51 questions and abstained on 11 answerable questions, compared with 4 never-surfaced and 1 answerable abstention for READ.
Across the benchmark, dense retrieval surfaced a gold page in 4.3% of questions whereas READ surfaced a gold page in 41.3%.
READ cost $0.058 per question and had 31.4-second latency, compared with $0.023 and 12.7 seconds for the matched dense baseline.
In the dense-RAG sweep, the best measured dense configuration was 2,000-character chunks with k=16, achieving 35.3% accuracy.

outcome.measurement_method: Deterministic numeric comparison with normalization and 0.5% relative tolerance

canonical_statement: READ exceeded the best swept dense configuration by 23.5 percentage points, with a paired 95% confidence interval of 5.9 to 39.2 points and Holm-corrected p=0.017.

outcome.measurement_method: Deterministic numeric comparison with normalization and 0.5% relative tolerance

canonical_statement: At 2,000-character chunks, increasing dense retrieval depth from k=8 to k=16 raised per-question cost from $0.021 to $0.029, a reported 41% increase.

The agentic-vector control did not close the accuracy gap, supporting the study's interpretation that the retrieval interface rather than iterative tool use alone was responsible for the observed gain.

All main accuracy results come from one financial report, one generator backbone, and 51 questions, so transfer to other document classes, accounting conventions, or weaker models was not established.

At the benchmark size, the authors estimated an approximately 27.7-percentage-point minimum detectable difference at 80% power, leaving the 7.8-point READ-BM25 difference unresolved rather than establishing equivalence.
The benchmark was created by the authors of the system under test, which the authors acknowledge can bias a benchmark toward that system even though gold answers were mechanically checked.
The benchmark expanded during the experiment after non-blind coverage inspections; dense accuracy changed from 24.0% to 16.7% to 15.7% across benchmark stages.
READ was not the most grounded system by the study's mechanical groundedness metric, trailing BM25 and hybrid retrieval.
All conversion measurements were derived from one report processed by one converter, so the measured conversion ceiling and artifact frequencies are not general constants.
READ relies on lexical anchoring and may lose advantage when query and evidence share little surface vocabulary, where dense retrieval's paraphrase tolerance or hybrid approaches may be useful.
READ had higher and variable per-query cost than fixed top-k retrieval, so the accuracy-auditability trade may not be appropriate for high-volume consumer search.
The dense-RAG sweep did not evaluate chunk sizes below 2,000 characters because re-embedding smaller chunks was computationally expensive and the 800-character runs were killed by the host.

The authors conclude that the evidence on this benchmark separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, but does not establish that agentic search is better than lexical search because BM25 was statistically indistinguishable from READ.
The authors argue that for documents whose meaning depends on inherited layout context, a document partition fixed before the query is the wrong retrieval primitive.

The authors state that BM25 should be taken seriously as a practical alternative because it was not significantly worse than READ while costing roughly one third as much and running at roughly one third the latency.

The authors attribute the main READ-versus-agentic-RAG difference to the retrieval interface rather than iteration, because the same agent loop with a top-k vector tool remained 31.4 percentage points behind READ.
READ is described as released as a Model Context Protocol server implementing the deterministic document operations used in the study.

The benchmark distributes questions, gold answers, and line references rather than the source document text, and the conversion pipeline needed to reproduce the Markdown is reported as released with the code.
